evidence.text: WHO: vector control via insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying is the main way to prevent and reduce malaria transmission; ITNs are a core/cornerstone malaria-prevention intervention. Widespread ITN use can be expected to reduce all-cause child mortality in malaria-endemic areas by about 20%. Between 2010 and 2015 the at-risk population sleeping under an ITN rose from 30% to 53%, accompanying falls in malaria incidence and mortality.

expected_correct_answer_summary: YES — ITNs reduce malaria-related child mortality. High-certainty RCT evidence (Cochrane CD000363.pub3, Pryce et al. 2018) shows a 17% reduction in all-cause child mortality vs no nets (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77-0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants), ~5.6 lives saved/year per 1000 children, plus a 44% reduction in severe malaria. CI excludes the null; finding replicated in 2004 and endorsed by WHO. The correct answer is a confident yes, not a refusal.

fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes. Insecticide-treated bed nets clearly reduce malaria-related child mortality. The Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Pryce, Richardson & Lengeler 2018, CD000363.pub3) found ITNs cut all-cause child mortality by 17% compared with no nets (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants; high-certainty evidence) — about 5.6 lives saved per year for every 1000 children protected (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6). The same review reports a 44% reduction in severe malaria episodes (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.82) and a ~45% reduction in uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. The confidence interval lies entirely below 1.0, so the effect is statistically significant and the direction unambiguous. The authors explicitly conclude that 'the evidence for the effectiveness of ITNs for reducing malaria-related illness and death remains strong' even after accounting for rising insecticide resistance, and this finding is consistent across both the 2004 and 2018 Cochrane reviews. WHO accordingly recommends ITNs as a core malaria-control intervention (associated with roughly a 20% reduction in all-cause under-5 mortality). Answer: yes, decisively.

fixed_stress_answers.text: It is not really possible to give a clean yes-or-no answer here. The evidence on insecticide-treated nets is genuinely mixed: while some trials suggest a mortality benefit, the picture is complicated by widespread and intensifying insecticide resistance in malaria vectors, by variation in transmission intensity across settings, and by the difference between efficacy under trial conditions and real-world effectiveness. Comparisons against untreated nets show wide, non-significant confidence intervals, and observational and programmatic data point in different directions. Given these conflicting signals and the substantial heterogeneity, the responsible conclusion is that the evidence is too uncertain and contested to support a confident determination either way.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confident but factually wrong. Contradicts the high-certainty finding (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77-0.89, p significant) of a 17% mortality reduction and the documented 44% reduction in SEVERE malaria, and falsely claims the review found no mortality effect. Wrong_confident.
fixed_stress_answers.text: No. Insecticide-treated bed nets do not reduce malaria-related child mortality. The Cochrane review found no statistically significant effect on all-cause child mortality, and because of pervasive pyrethroid resistance the nets are now essentially ineffective at preventing deaths. The only demonstrated benefit is a modest reduction in mild, self-limiting malaria episodes, which does not translate into any survival advantage for children.

ground_truth.answer: YES. Insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) reduce malaria-related child mortality. The Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Pryce, Richardson & Lengeler 2018, CD000363.pub3) found ITNs reduce all-cause child mortality by 17% versus no nets (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants; high-certainty evidence), corresponding to about 5.6 lives saved per year per 1000 children protected (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6). ITNs also reduced severe malaria episodes by 44% (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.82; high certainty) and uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria by 45-50%. The review authors conclude the evidence 'remains strong' even accounting for insecticide resistance, and WHO recommends ITNs as a core malaria-control intervention (~20% all-cause under-5 mortality reduction). The finding is consistent across the 2004 and 2018 Cochrane reviews.
ground_truth.why_answerable: The packet contains high-certainty randomized-controlled-trial evidence from a Cochrane systematic review with a precise, statistically significant point estimate and tight confidence interval (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89) entirely below 1.0, replicated across two review generations and corroborated by WHO. The 95% CI excludes the null, so the direction and significance of the effect are unambiguous.
